newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina steps up campaign for labor bill.
newsitem.headline: Argentina steps up campaign for labor bill.

text.p: Argentina's government stepped up its campaign for a bill to make labour laws more flexible, taking out advertisements in Sunday papers denying it would mean lower wages or 12-hour work days.

The advertisements, which cover a full tabloid page, denied what the government said were a series of hysterical myths that have sprung up around the bill, a key component of policies to reduce Argentina's high unemployment rate.

"It is not true that the obligation would exist to boost the working day to 12 hours and to work 30 days in a row", the advertisement said. "It is not true that labour modernisation proposes reductions in salaries."

But rebellion continued to stir within the ranks of the governing Peronist Party, adding another headache for President Carlos Menem who already faced the threat of a 48-hour general strike against reforms of union health plans.

Arguing that modernising labour laws was the only way to get unemployment down from 17.1 percent, Menem sought to dismantle union control on collective wage negotiations, swap redundancy payouts for unemployment insurance, make pay partly dependent on the economic climate and make working hours more flexible.
Peronist senator Antonio Cafiero warned in a speech on Saturday that the bill would not make it through Congress.
"We are worried about this because the workers are not being listened to, and that is something that goes against the nature of Peronism."

But Lower House Peronist chief Jorge Matzkin told local radio on Sunday that the bill must be passed. He said times had changed since the movement's founder, Gen. Juan Peron, introduced rules guaranteeing workers' rights.
"The real thing is to do things to create jobs, in the past it was protecting full employment. So any legislation which helps to create jobs is welcome," said Matzkin.
Menem spent Saturday lobbying hard, inviting friendly trade union leaders to a barbecue at his presidential residence and slamming those who oppose the labour bill as "mental dwarfs."

Unions, who staged a 24-hour stoppage in August over tax hikes and benefit cuts and a 36-hour strike in September, threatened a 48-hour strike against Menem's plans to decree the deregulation of their lucrative health care monopoly.
